lesson.subtitle: Lesson 40 — Getting Used to It
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 40 — Getting Used to It
lesson.grammar_point: be used to / get used to + -ing for adapting to something new (I'm used to speaking / I'm getting used to it / you'll get used to it)

listenings.text: Here are two small words that confuse a lot of learners: used to. They can mean three different things. First, I used to, plus a verb, is about the past. I used to live in Rio means I lived there before, but not now. Second, I'm used to, plus i-n-g, means that something is normal for me. I'm used to working late, so it isn't hard. Third, I'm getting used to is the process: something is new, and it's becoming normal, step by step. I'm getting used to my new job. One more thing. After be used to and get used to, we use the i-n-g form, or a noun. So say, I'm used to speaking English. Don't say, I'm used to speak English. And if something is still strange for you, don't worry. You'll get used to it.

Hi Vanessa, it's Marcos, from Toronto. It's been three months, so I wanted to tell you how it's going. The first few weeks were hard. I wasn't used to the cold at all, and I felt really self-conscious at work, because everyone speaks so fast. But gradually, things are changing. I'm getting used to the accent, and now I'm used to taking the subway at seven, in the snow! The thing I still can't get used to is dinner at six in the evening. That's far too early for a Brazilian. Anyway, here's my advice for you: don't hold back in your meetings. You'll get used to it faster than you think. Talk soon!

extra_audio.text: First, something new feels awkward, and I hold back. Then I try it again, even if I feel self-conscious. After that, I gradually get used to it. Next, I'm used to it, and it becomes second nature. In the end, I look back and see that I've come a long way.

paras: Anyone who learns a language as an adult goes through the awkward phase. You understand much more than you can say, you feel self-conscious about your accent, and in meetings you hold back, even when you have a good idea.

The good news is that the awkward phase does not last forever. Your brain gets used to almost anything if you repeat it often enough. The first video call in English feels strange. The tenth feels a little less strange. By the fiftieth, you are used to it, and you hardly notice.

The secret is not to wait until you feel ready. People who wait for confidence often stay inside their comfort zone for years. People who speak first, and feel confident later, get used to the discomfort, and gradually speaking becomes second nature.
So if you are halfway through a course, look back and compare. Are you used to things that scared you at the beginning? Then you have come a long way. Keep it up. -- Marta, language coach
